narrative: Today's batch centred on climate-driven range dynamics and behavioural responses to environmental stress. In Ecography, a multispecies seed-addition experiment found range shifts lag climate velocity at species' leading edges but not their trailing edges, while microhabitat variability was shown to override macroclimatic suitability in predicting range establishment elsewhere in the same journal. Drought reshaped animal movement and social structure across several papers: elephants curtailed movement and shifted habitat selection across drought timescales, and a carnivore guild intensified dominant-competitor avoidance under dry conditions, while a striking natural experiment found COVID lockdowns weakened mammal avoidance of humans by 36%, with carnivores shifting roughly twice as much as herbivores. Invasion ecology contributed two notable findings — reduced litter allelochemicals were shown to facilitate further alien species establishment, supporting the invasional meltdown hypothesis, and selection on genome architecture was linked to genome size evolution in globally invasive ragweed. On the conservation and grazing front, a 38-year rewetting experiment restored peat accumulation and near-natural vegetation to forestry-drained fens, while a comparative study warned that measures reducing carnivore predation on livestock could unintentionally intensify rangeland grazing pressure. Methods contributions were strong this cycle, with new tools for zero-shot bioacoustic classification of frog calls, LiDAR-based 3D tree morphometrics, and Bayesian mortality estimation from imperfect carcass surveys. Finally, evolutionary biology returned to classic questions, tracing pathogen seasonal timing to priority effects and stabilising selection, and revisiting Gloger's and Bogert's rules across plumage patterns in over ten thousand bird species.
